questions.prompt: Why are break-glass accounts excluded from Conditional Access by design?
options: So they remain usable when Conditional Access, MFA, or federation is exactly what has failed
Because they are never actually used
questions.explanation: The exclusion is the point -- these accounts exist to restore access when the protective controls themselves are broken. It is also precisely what makes them attractive as backdoors.

questions.prompt: What is the control that makes break-glass accounts safe to have?
options: Alerting on every sign-in at high priority, since there is no routine use and a single authentication is an incident until proven otherwise
Disabling them when not in use
questions.explanation: Given they should never authenticate outside a declared emergency, a single successful sign-in is directly actionable with no further correlation needed.

questions.prompt: What is the more durable attacker variant of break-glass abuse?
options: Creating an ordinary-looking privileged account and adding it to Conditional Access exclusion lists, giving it the same protection profile
questions.explanation: Nothing about the account itself looks unusual -- the anomaly lives in the policy configuration rather than the identity, which is why exclusion-list diffing is the needed detection.

questions.prompt: Why should break-glass accounts be cloud-only rather than synced from on-premises AD?
options: Synced accounts cannot hold Global Administrator
So an on-premises compromise cannot reach them
Cloud-only accounts are cheaper to license
Synced accounts cannot be excluded from Conditional Access
questions.explanation: Keeping them outside the sync boundary means a full on-premises Active Directory compromise does not automatically deliver the emergency access accounts as well.
